title: A State Court Authorization Couldn't Cover a County Courthouse — the Sheriff Called the Contract Void
dek: A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even when all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays forever — the justice system can pay damages, but it can't restore a clean name.
why: This episode explains the fragility of an 'authorization contract' more clearly than any exploit: the building's owner can override all paperwork, and legal accountability is nearly blocked by immunity. Anyone in security outsourcing or vendor projects should pause here.
who: Physical security testing teams, legal counsel for security vendors, and anyone who enters a site with a client's authorization; also tech founders who want to understand the American game of governmental immunity.
skip: The first half hour covers lock-picking techniques and access control details — technical fun, but if you're impatient, jump to 35:18 to see the conflict erupt.

points.h: Verbal agreements mean no authorization at all
points.body: The rulebook is only 28 pages, which makes it easy to think the written contract locks everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed agreements were almost all made verbally over the phone; if everything were written down, the contract would be a hundred pages long and no one would sign it. That compromise planted a landmine: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the verbal scope didn't cover that building — so procedurally, they walked into a building with 'no authorization.' The sheriff's later claim of 'no authorization' wasn't rooted in technology but in a contract that couldn't cover every verbal conversation.

points.h: The building's owner outranks the authorization letter
points.body: Before the sheriff arrived, they were confident because the contract explicitly stated state court authorization. But the sheriff's reaction was simple: they don't own this courthouse, I don't care if you have a contract. Gary and Justin realized that the right to use a building and the right to contract are separate; no matter how formal the state court's contract was, it couldn't make entry decisions for the county courthouse's owner. The atmosphere shifted from relaxed to arrest, and they hadn't even worried beforehand because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

points.h: The judge heard truth as lies
points.body: The judge told Gary, 'You must think I'm stupid' — her reasoning was: if the state government had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, would have known; since she didn't know, it could only be a lie. Gary later said that this judge, who faced criminals' lies daily, could no longer distinguish truth. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-style contract looks even more false. Professional reports and legal procedures were useless in this scenario.

points.h: Dropped charges don't erase the record
points.body: On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but their criminal records will forever show they were arrested for burglary. Justin said they were deprived of their rights without due process — in many U.S. background checks, an arrest record is as visible as a conviction. Dropping charges only means no prosecution; it can't erase the collateral consequences of that arrest: job applications, border crossings, security clearances — that episode follows them. The innocence they won in the criminal fight was only half won.

points.h: Government immunity blocks accountability for its own mistakes
points.body: Seeking accountability was harder than imagined. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor, and the judge, but the system presented two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in their official capacity, and sovereign immunity says you can't sue the government without its consent. The state court first dismissed the case — because the state government was the defendant; the federal court then kicked it back to the state, which dismissed it again. This isn't judges deciding cases; it's that the system has no entry point for 'the government was wrong.' The only thing victims can sue is the office, not the person holding it; the sheriff personally doesn't pay a cent. Judicial checks and balances here become an idle adjective.

points.h: Winning the legal lottery buys back a sliver of dignity
points.body: Almost every wrongful arrest case dies the same way: over 95% are dismissed on qualified immunity grounds, and most of the rest end in zero damages or government victory. Getting more than $50,000 in damages is like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly held for weeks or months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, but their evidence was airtight, and at arbitration they finally got a rare public statement: it wasn't a question of whether they'd win, but how much they'd get. As trial approached, the county offered $300,000 each, $600,000 total, to settle. But for them, that money can't buy back the half-life already written into their records.

A legal doctrine that prevents private parties from suing the government without its consent.
